name: Design a Real-Time OLAP Analytics Engine
intent: Answer slice-and-dice questions over billions of fresh events in under a second, while the events are still arriving, and keep a year of history affordable.
codeTitle: rolled-up segments with dictionary columns, bitmap filters and scatter-gather
finalIntro: An event arriving, and a dashboard question answered a few seconds later.
prompt: Design the analytics engine behind a product dashboard, in the style of Druid or ClickHouse. Hundreds of thousands of events arrive every second from a stream, and old data is also loaded in batches. Analysts filter and group by country, device, campaign and time, and expect results in under a second, including events from the last few seconds.
functional: Ingest events from a stream and from batch files
Filter and group by dimensions such as country, device and campaign, and aggregate counts, sums and distinct counts
Query any time range, from the last minute to the last year
Make new events queryable within a few seconds
Keep recent data fast and older data cheap
Reload or correct a day of data from a batch job
nonFunctional: Most dashboard queries return in under a second, and the slowest ones in a few seconds
Ingest 500,000 events per second, and tens of dashboard queries per second
Storage for a year of history costs a small fraction of the raw data
Losing a machine loses no data and does not stop queries
No single query can slow everyone else down
Results are consistent: an event is counted once, even if the stream redelivers it

firstAttempt.text: One SQL database with a row-oriented events table. Every event is inserted as a row, with indexes on time and the main dimensions. A dashboard query is a SELECT with a WHERE on the filters and a GROUP BY, scanning the matching rows.
limits: A row store reads every column of every row, even though a query needs only two or three columns
Billions of rows per day make the table and its indexes enormous, and every insert updates several indexes
Each query scans billions of rows on one machine, so one dashboard takes minutes and a few dashboards stop the inserts
Raw events are kept forever on expensive disks, although almost nobody asks for per-event detail
There is one machine, so it is a single point of failure and has a hard size limit

steps.title: Store columns in immutable, time-partitioned segments
steps.problem: A query that sums one number grouped by country should not have to read every field of every event, and one giant table is slow to scan and to maintain.
steps.fix: Cut the data into segments, each covering a slice of time, such as one hour, and write each segment once and never change it. Inside a segment every column is stored on its own. A text column like country is dictionary-encoded: the distinct values are listed once and each row stores a small integer. For each dictionary value a bitmap marks the rows that hold it, so a filter such as country in (DE, FR) and device is ios becomes a bitwise OR and AND of a few bitmaps, and only the rows that remain are read. A query touches only the columns it names, and similar values next to each other compress very well.
steps.tradeoff: Scans are fast and the data is several times smaller. Rows cannot be updated in place, a single-row lookup is slow, and building a segment takes effort, so data is written in batches and corrections replace whole segments.

steps.title: Roll events up while ingesting
steps.problem: Nobody asks about one click, but billions of them per day are stored, scanned and paid for, and most dashboards only need counts and sums per minute and per dimension.
steps.fix: A stream consumer reads the events and merges those that share the same time bucket and dimension values into one row holding a count, a sum and other aggregates. With a one-minute bucket and the dimensions country, device and campaign, many events share one row, and 10 to 100 times fewer rows is common. Distinct counts and percentiles are kept as small mergeable sketches (fixed-size summaries that give approximate answers) rather than as lists. Fresh rows are held in memory in a real-time segment, which is queryable at once and is written out as an immutable segment when its time window closes.
steps.tradeoff: Storage and scan work shrink by the rollup ratio and results arrive within seconds. The original events are gone, so a question that needs a dimension that was not kept cannot be answered, and a column with huge cardinality (very many distinct values), such as the user id, destroys the ratio.

steps.title: Add batch loading, deep storage and a segment catalog
steps.problem: Real-time ingestion can miss or double count events, late events arrive after their window closed, and a year of history needs a durable home that does not depend on any one machine.
steps.fix: Every finished segment is uploaded to deep storage such as object storage, which is the durable copy, and recorded in a segment catalog with its time range and version. The stream consumer commits its offsets (its position in the stream) together with the segment it publishes, so after a crash it resumes from the stored offsets and an event is never counted twice. A batch job can rebuild a day from the raw files and publish new segments for the same interval with a higher version. The catalog switches queries to the new version atomically, and the old segments are dropped afterwards.
steps.tradeoff: History is durable, corrections and late data are possible, and any machine can be replaced by reloading its segments from deep storage. There is now a catalog to keep consistent and a set of versions to garbage-collect, and the freshest data can briefly be present in two forms.

steps.title: Answer queries by scatter-gather over segments
steps.problem: A year of segments cannot be scanned by one process, and most queries only need a small part of it.
steps.fix: A broker receives the query and asks the catalog which segments overlap the requested time range, which prunes most of the year at once. It sends the query to the data nodes that hold those segments, and each node scans its own segments in parallel using the bitmaps and returns a small partial result: a group key with partial counts and sums. The broker merges the partials, adding counts and sums and combining sketches, applies the final sort and limit, and replies. Segments are spread over nodes and replicated, so one node dying only means its replicas answer.
steps.tradeoff: Latency is the slowest participant plus the merge, and capacity grows by adding nodes. Aggregates must be mergeable: counts, sums, minimum and maximum merge exactly, and distinct counts and percentiles merge only as approximate sketches. A few slow nodes dominate the tail, which hedged requests and replicas help to hide.

steps.title: Tier hot and cold data
steps.problem: Almost all queries ask about the last few days, yet keeping a year of segments on fast local disks and in memory costs many times more than it brings in.
steps.fix: Place recent segments on hot nodes with fast SSDs and several replicas, and let a rule move older ones to cold nodes that have cheaper, larger disks and fewer replicas. Cold segments can be served from deep storage with the data fetched on demand and cached, and very old data can be merged into larger segments with a coarser rollup, such as hourly instead of by minute. Retention rules drop what nobody needs. The broker sends a query to the hot tier first and to the cold tier only if the time range reaches that far.
steps.tradeoff: Cost drops by a large factor and the common queries stay fast. A query over old data is slower, moving data between tiers uses bandwidth, and coarser rollups mean old data has less detail than new data.

steps.title: Limit cardinality and protect the cluster from heavy queries
steps.problem: A dimension with millions of distinct values, such as a user id, makes dictionaries huge and rollup useless, and a single group-by over it can use all the memory of the cluster.
steps.fix: Keep high-cardinality fields out of the rollup key and store them as sketches for distinct counts instead. Cap the number of distinct values a dimension may have, and bucket or truncate values such as raw URLs. At query time enforce a time limit, a cap on rows scanned and on groups returned, and return only the top groups, which is approximate when merging partial top lists. Give each team a quota and run slow reports in a separate pool, so one expensive query cannot starve the dashboards.
steps.tradeoff: The cluster stays predictable and cheap. Some questions are answered approximately or refused, analysts must learn which dimensions are queryable, and a limit set too low blocks legitimate work.

failures.scenario: A data node dies during a query
failures.impact: Its partial results never arrive, so the totals would be too small.
failures.answer: Every segment has replicas on other nodes, and the broker retries the missing segments there, so the answer is complete. If a result is incomplete, the broker marks it as partial instead of presenting it as exact. The cluster then copies the lost replicas from deep storage to other nodes.

failures.scenario: The ingest worker crashes and the stream redelivers events
failures.impact: Events may be counted twice, or lost if offsets were saved too early.
failures.answer: Offsets are stored in the same step that publishes the segment, so after a restart the worker resumes from the last published offsets. Events that were only in memory are read from the stream again, and a repeated segment of the same interval and version simply replaces itself.

failures.scenario: Someone adds the user id as a dimension
failures.impact: Rollup collapses to 1x, dictionaries and bitmaps for millions of values fill memory, and storage nearly equals the raw data.
failures.answer: Ingestion checks the cardinality of every dimension and rejects or truncates values beyond a cap. A distinct count of users is kept as a sketch in each row instead, which costs about a kilobyte per row, and per-user questions go to a different system built for lookups.

failures.scenario: A group-by over a huge range floods the cluster
failures.impact: All nodes spend their time on one report, and the live dashboards time out.
failures.answer: The broker enforces a deadline and row limits, and runs the query in its own lane with a concurrency cap per team. The report is cancelled when the deadline passes, and its owner is told to narrow the range or use a coarser, pre-rolled table.

alternatives.title: What is stored

options.name: Raw events only
options.pro: Any question can be answered, and nothing is lost
options.con: Storage and scans are huge, and every query pays for detail it does not need

options.name: Rolled-up rows
options.pro: Tens of times smaller and faster, and dashboards come back in milliseconds
options.con: Questions about dimensions that were dropped cannot be answered

options.name: Both: rollup hot, raw in cheap storage
options.pro: Fast dashboards and a way to reprocess
options.con: Two copies and a job to keep them consistent

alternatives.pick: Rolled-up rows for serving, with raw files kept in cheap object storage for backfills.

alternatives.title: How new events become queryable

options.name: Streaming into in-memory segments
options.con: Needs offset handling and a memory-resident, queryable real-time part

alternatives.pick: Streaming into a real-time segment, merged into immutable segments as windows close.

alternatives.title: Exact or approximate distinct counts

options.name: Exact, with sets of ids
options.con: Memory grows with cardinality, and sets from many segments are expensive to merge

options.name: Sketches (HyperLogLog)
options.pro: A few kilobytes whatever the cardinality, and they merge by taking maxima
options.con: An error of about 1 to 2%, and no way to list the members

alternatives.pick: Sketches for dashboards, exact counts only for small, billing-grade questions on a slower path.

alternatives.title: Where the data and compute live

options.name: Local disks on each node
options.pro: The fastest scans, with no network fetches
options.con: Scaling and replacing nodes means copying data

options.name: Compute reading object storage with local caches
options.pro: Compute scales independently, and nodes are disposable
options.con: Cold queries pay network latency, and caches must be warm

alternatives.pick: Local disks for the hot tier, and object storage with caching for the cold tier.

roles.label: Dashboards
roles.description: Analysts and apps that run queries.

roles.label: Query broker
roles.description: Receives queries, prunes segments and merges partial results.

roles.label: Workers
roles.description: Ingest, rollup, hot and cold data nodes, and query limits.

roles.label: State
roles.description: Segments, the catalog, batch files and deep storage.

quiz.question: A dashboard sums revenue by country over 3 billion rows of an events table that has 40 columns, stored row by row. It takes minutes, and a few concurrent dashboards stall the inserts. What is the best change to the storage layout?
options: Add a composite index on country, time and revenue, so the group-by can be answered from the index alone
Store the data in columnar, time-partitioned segments, so a query reads only the columns it names
Partition the events table by month and run each dashboard on a read replica of its own partition
Move to a larger machine with more memory, so that the whole table stays cached in RAM for the queries
quiz.explanation: A row store reads all 40 columns of every row to use two, while columns stored separately and compressed cut that work by an order of magnitude. A composite index slows every insert and still touches billions of entries, and partitions, replicas or more RAM keep the row layout.

quiz.question: An OLAP engine ingests 500,000 events per second, which is 30 million per minute. Rollup groups them by minute, country (about 150 values), device (4) and campaign (100). A product manager now asks for exact unique users per country on the same dashboard. What is the best way to do this?
options: Add the user id to the rollup key, so each row counts one user and distinct users can be counted exactly
Keep the list of user ids in every rolled-up row, and take their union when the broker merges the rows
Stop rolling up the last 7 days, and count the users from the raw events whenever the dashboard asks
Store a mergeable distinct-count sketch in each rolled-up row, accepting an error of about 1 to 2 percent in the counts
quiz.explanation: The key has at most about 60,000 combinations per minute, a rollup of at least 500 to one, and the user id would destroy that. A sketch of a few kilobytes keeps the ratio and merges by taking maxima. Lists of ids grow with cardinality and are costly to merge, and raw scans bring back the cost rollup was meant to remove.

quiz.question: A stream consumer builds segments, publishes them to deep storage and commits its offsets back to the stream as a separate step. It crashes after it publishes a segment but before it commits the offset. After restart, the totals on the dashboard are too high. What design prevents this?
options: Commit the stream offset first and publish the segment second, so that a crash can never leave events counted twice
Run a nightly query that finds duplicate events by id and subtracts them from the totals shown on the dashboards
Store the stream offsets in the same atomic step that publishes the segment to deep storage
Publish each segment twice, to two different locations, so that a crash cannot lose the only copy of the data
quiz.explanation: If the offsets are saved in the same step that publishes the segment, a restart resumes exactly where published data ends, so nothing is counted twice or skipped. Committing first reverses the failure and loses events, a nightly repair leaves wrong numbers on screen all day, and duplicate copies do not fix the offset gap.
